Assignment 2, due Thursday 2024-02-15 at 23:59

A.2.1
Mediocre cuts

Recall that a cut in a graph
G
is a partition of the vertices
into sets
S
and
T
, where the size of the cut is the number of
edges with one endpoint in each set.

Given a graph
G
with
n
vertices and
m
edges, we’d like to
construct a cut with size as close as possible to
m/2
.
We will consider two algorithms that generate
0
-
1
random variables

X_{v}
for each vertex
v
, such that
v
is in
S
if
X_{v}=0
and
v
is
in
T
if
X_{v}=1
.

1.

In the first algorithm,
X_{v}
is simply an independent
fair coin-flip for each
v
.

Prove or disprove: This algorithm produces a cut of size
m/2\pm o(m)
with constant nonzero probability.

2.

In this second algorithm, the independent fair coins
are replaced by pairwise independent coins,
constructed as
in §
5.1.2.1
:
Generate
k=\lceil\lg(n+1)\rceil
independent fair random bits

Y_{1},\dots,Y_{k}
, assign each vertex
v
a unique non-empty
subset
A_{v}
of these bits, and let
X_{v}=\bigoplus_{i\in A_{v}}Y_{i}
.

Prove or disprove: This algorithm produces a cut of size
m/2\pm o(m)
with constant nonzero probability.

Solution

1.

We’ll give a proof using Chebyshev’s inequality.

For each edge
uv
let
Z_{uv}=X_{u}\oplus X_{v}
be the
indicator variable for the event that
uv
is in the
cut. Let
S=\sum_{uv}Z_{uv}
be the size of the cut.

We have
\E\left[{S}\right]=\sum\E\left[{Z_{uv}}\right]=m/2
.

To compute
\Variance\left[{S}\right]
, we will first show that the
variables
Z_{uv}
are pairwise-independent.
This holds trivially for any variables corresponding
to non-incident edges. For the case of two incident
edges
Z_{uv}
and
Z_{vw}
,
observe that
\E\left[{Z_{vw}}\;\middle|\;{Z_{uv}}\right]=1/2
, because
whatever value
X_{v}
has, adding
X_{w}
yields
0
or

1
with equal probability. So
Z_{uv}
and
Z_{vw}
are
independent as well.

Since the
Z_{uv}
are pairwise-independent,
\Variance\left[{S}\right]=\sum\Variance\left[{Z_{uv}}\right]=m/4
.
Chebyshev then says

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{\left\lvert S-m/2\right\rvert\geq\sqrt{m}}\right]

\displaystyle\leq\frac{m/4}{(\sqrt{m})^{2}}=\frac{1}{4}.

This gives a
3/4
chance of getting

S
in the range
m/2\pm\sqrt{m}=m/2\pm o(m)
.

2.

For this version we will give a disproof, by
constructing a family of arbitrarily large graphs
where the algorithm generates a cut of size
0
or
m

with equal probability.

Fix some
n
, and create an edge
uv
for each pair of
vertices
u
and
v
with
A_{u}=A_{v}\triangle\left\{{1}\right\}
. This will give a total of
m=n/2
edges.
Each such edge will have
X_{u}=X_{v}\oplus Y_{1}
; this will
put
uv
in the cut precisely when
Y_{1}=1
. So the
cut will have
0
edges with probability
1/2
and
m

edges with probability
1/2
.

In neither case is the size of the cut within
o(m)

of
m/2
, so the algorithm does not guarantee this
with nonzero probability.

A.2.2
Training costs

A total of
n
workers arrive at a site in blocks of size
n_{1},n_{2},\dots,n_{k}
, where
\sum n_{i}=n
. After the
i
-th block
arrives, one of the
n_{1}+n_{2}+\dots+n_{i}
workers now on site is chosen
uniformly at random to be the leader. If the leader arrived
previously (was one of the
n_{1}+n_{2}+\dots+n_{i-1}
workers already
at the site), they are said to be
experienced
and require
no training. If the leader was one of the most recent
n_{i}

arrivals, they are
inexperienced
and must be trained. We’d
like to get an estimate of the worst-case expected cost of training
inexperienced leaders, assuming that an adversary chooses the
sizes and number of the blocks
n_{1},\dots,n_{k}
, and show that the
actual cost is likely to be close to the expected cost.

We consider two different models for the cost of training an
inexperienced leader.

1.

In the first model, an inexperienced leader remedies
their ignorance by calling the help line 1-800-LEADER, at
a cost of one unit.

Show an upper bound
f(n)
on the worst-case
expected total training cost for this model, and show that
there is are constants
c>0
and
c^{\prime}<1
such that actual cost in this
worst case is within
f(n)\pm c^{\prime}f(n)
for sufficiently
large
n

with probability at least
1-O(n^{-c})
.

2.

This part of the problem contained an error
and has been withdrawn. You do not need to supply a
solution to this part of the problem and will be given
full credit for it.

Solution

1.

First we need to figure out the worst-case
choice of
n_{1},\dots,n_{k}
.

For any particular choice of the block sizes, the
expected cost is

\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{n_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{i}n_{j}}.

It is not hard to see that this quantity is maximized
when
k=n
and
n_{i}=1
for all
i
. The proof is to
observe that if any
n_{i}>1
, it can be replaced by
consecutive blocks of size
n_{i}-1
and
1
, giving
an expected cost for these two new blocks of

\displaystyle\frac{n_{i}-1}{\sum_{j=i}n_{i}-1}+\frac{1}{\sum_{j=i}^{i}n_{i}}

\displaystyle>\frac{n_{i}-1}{\sum_{j=i}n_{i}}+\frac{1}{\sum_{j=i}^{i}n_{i}}=\frac{n_{i}}{\sum_{j=i}n_{i}},

which increases the expected total cost.

Setting each
n_{i}=1
, the expected total cost is

\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i}

\displaystyle=H_{n}=\Theta(\log n).

Let
X_{i}
be the training cost for the
i
-th block.
Then each
X_{i}
is an independent Bernoulli random
variable and
S=\sum X_{i}
has known expectation

\mu=H_{n}=\Theta(\log n)
,
so we can use the two-sided Chernoff bound
(
5.2.7
) to get

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{\left\lvert S-\mu\right\rvert\geq(1/2)\mu}\right]

\displaystyle\leq 2e^{-\mu/12}=2e^{-\Theta(\log n)}=O(n^{-c}),

for some
c>0
.

But then
S
lies between
(1/2)\mu
and
(3/2)\mu
with
probability
1-O(n^{-c})
, giving the desired bound.

A.3
Assignment 3, due Thursday 2024-02-29 at 23:59

A.3.1
A robot rendezvous problem

A warehouse for a large online retailer has
n
packages, each of
which has a distinct tracking number
t_{i}\in\left\{{0,\dots,t-1}\right\}
.
Each package
starts out in the possession of one of
n
warehouse robots and
needs
to be transferred to one of
n
corresponding delivery drones to be delivered.
We will refer to the robots and drones collectively as

workers
.

Unfortunately there are only
m<n
landing pads for the
drones, and the scheduling system that assigns packages to
the workers does not know about the landing pads.

Instead, each worker knows only
n
,
m
,
t
, the unique tracking number

t_{i}
for its assigned package, whether it is a robot or a drone, and up to

b
bits of randomness that is shared between all the
workers, where
b
is polylogarithmic in
t
(meaning
that
b=O(\log^{c}t)
for some
c
).
1
1

1

There is a very
technical issue here involving how the bound on the number of
bits interpreted.
One extreme is that we have
b
bits of randomness and all
2^{b}

possible bit strings are equally likely. The other extreme is that
some algorithm generates a random variable or collection of random
variables that collectively take on at most
2^{b}
distinct
possible values (and thus can be encoded in
b
bits), but there
is no requirement that each possible value is equally likely.
While the problem is solvable in either model, there are fewer
details to worry about in the second model, so you should feel
free to assume, for example, that you can encode a six-sided die
in 3 bits by assigning
0
probability to
000
and
111
and

1/6
probability to each of the remaining six bit vectors.

Using this information, it must choose one of
the
m
landing pads
0,\dots,m-1
in one of
k
rounds

0,\dots,k-1
. If exactly one robot and its
corresponding drone arrive at a particular pad during a round, the
package is transferred successfully. If a robot meets a drone
expecting a different package, or if two robots or two drones
attempt to use the same pad during the same round, the transfer
fails and any workers choosing that pad in that round must try again at a later
round. Each worker has no ability to communicate with
other workers beyond being able to detect if a transfer it attempted
failed or not.

It is clear that
k
must be at least
\lceil n/m\rceil
for it to be
possible to deliver all the packages even with perfect
coordination. Show that this is almost sufficient, by giving an
algorithm that, for any fixed
c>0
, delivers all packages in
k=O\left((n/m)\log n\right)
rounds with probability at least
1-O(n^{-c})
.

Solution

We’ll have a sequence of
p=O(\log n)
phases of

\lceil 2n/m\rceil
rounds each, and in phase use a hash function to
assign each package to one of the
\ell=m\lceil 2n/m\rceil\geq 2n
slots
corresponding to a particular
combination of pad and round within the phase.

A complication is that we have limited randomness, which is
going to constrain what hash functions we can use. We’ll pick
an independent linear congruential hash function
h_{j}
for
each phase
j
, which requires
O(\log t)
bits of randomness
per phase or
O(\log t\log n)=O(\log^{2}t)
bits of
randomness across all phases. Tabulation hashing also works
(we want the version that adds table elements mod
\ell

rather than using XOR on bit vectors), but the bits per phase
goes up to
O(\log^{2}t)
giving
O(\log^{3}t)
overall.

In each phase, a remaining robot or drone assigned tracking
number
t_{i}
computes
h_{j}(t_{i})\in[\ell]
and goes to pad

h_{j}(t_{i})\bmod modm
during round
\lfloor h_{j}(t_{i})/m\rfloor

(numbering from
0
within the phase). Each pair of tracking
numbers
t_{i},t_{i^{\prime}}
produces a collision with probability

\Pr\left[{h_{j}(t_{i})=h_{j}(t_{i^{\prime}})}\right]\leq\frac{1}{\ell}
. Let
X_{j}
be
the number of robots left after
j
phases; then
X_{0}=n
and

\displaystyle\E\left[{X_{j+1}}\;\middle|\;{X_{j}}\right]

\displaystyle\leq 2\binom{X_{j}}{2}\frac{1}{\ell}\leq\frac{X_{j}^{2}}{2n}\leq\frac{X_{j}}{2}.

Here the
2
at the start accounts for the fact that each
collision may send up to two robots to the next phase, the

\binom{n}{2}
counts all the pairs of robots, and the last
step uses the bound
X_{j}\leq n
.

Iterating this inequality gives
\E\left[{X_{p}}\right]\leq n\cdot 2^{-p}
.
Set
p=\lg n
to get
\Pr\left[{X_{p}>0}\right]\leq\E\left[{X_{p}}\right]\leq 2^{-c\lg n}=n^{-c}
. This gives the desired error
probability in
c\lg n\lceil 2n/m\rceil=O(n\log n/m)
rounds.

A.3.2
A linked list

It is well-known that linked lists are terrible data structures,
with only
O(n)
guarantees on search time in the worst case.
However, for some distributions on elements, the average case
might be better.

Suppose we are given a set of
n
elements
1,\dots,n
, where at
each step element
i
is supplied with probability
p_{i}
.
Suppose that we insert each new element we see at the end of the
list, until eventually all
n
elements appear in the list. We
then sample a new element according to the given probability
distribution and ask what its expected position in the list is.

For a uniform distribution, this won’t help much: all
n!

orderings will be equally likely, and the expected position of a
random element is just
\frac{n+1}{2}=\Theta(n)
, which is (up to
constants)
no better than
the deterministic worst case. But for more skewed distributions we
may hope that more probable elements get inserted early, meaning
that the cost of searching for them will be less than for more
improbable elements.

For each of the following distributions, compute a tight (big-
\Theta
)
asymptotic bound on the expected cost to search for a random
element given by the distribution, assuming that we constructed
the list as described above by repeatedly sampling from the same
distribution.

1.

A geometric distribution with
p_{i}\propto 2^{-i}
.

2.

A
Zipf’s law
distribution with
p_{i}\propto\frac{1}{i}
.

Solution

Let’s do what we can for a generic distribution before getting
into the details of each distribution individually.

Let
A_{ij}
be the indicator variable for the event that
i

appears in the list at or before the same position as
j
(the
“at” part covers the case
A_{ii}
, which we take to be
1
).
Let
D_{i}
be the position of
i
in the list. Then
D_{i}=\sum_{j}A_{ji}
.

For
i\neq j
, we can compute
\E\left[{A_{ij}}\right]
by looking at
probability of seeing
i
conditioned on seeing
i
or
j
at
a particular step. This gives

\displaystyle\E\left[{A_{ij}}\right]

\displaystyle=\frac{p_{i}}{p_{i}+p_{j}},

\displaystyle\E\left[{D_{i}}\right]

\displaystyle=1+\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{p_{j}}{p_{i}+p_{j}}.

and thus

\displaystyle\E\left[{\text{search cost}}\right]

\displaystyle=\sum_{i}p_{i}\E\left[{D_{i}}\right]=1+\sum_{i}p_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{p_{j}}{p_{i}+p_{j}}.

Let’s see what happens to this for each of our given
distributions.

1.

When
p_{i}\propto 2^{-i}
, we have

\displaystyle p_{i}

\displaystyle=\frac{2^{-i}}{1-2^{-n-1}}=\Theta\left(2^{-i}\right).

Even better, the denominators cancel
while computing

\displaystyle\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{p_{j}}{p_{i}+p_{j}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{2^{-j}}{2^{-i}+2^{-j}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{j<i}\frac{2^{-j}}{2^{-i}+2^{-j}}+\sum_{j>i}\frac{2^{-j}}{2^{-i}+2^{-j}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{j<i}\frac{2^{-j}}{\Theta\left(2^{-j}\right)}+\sum_{j>i}\frac{2^{-j}}{\Theta\left(2^{-i}\right)}

\displaystyle=\sum_{j<i}\Theta(1)+\sum_{j>i}\Theta(2^{i-j})

\displaystyle=\Theta(i)+\Theta(1)

\displaystyle=\Theta(i).

We can now compute the expected search cost as

\displaystyle\sum_{i}p_{i}\E\left[{D_{i}}\right]

\displaystyle=1+\sum_{i}\Theta(2^{-i}i)=\Theta(1).

2.

In this case, we have

\displaystyle p_{i}

\displaystyle=\frac{1/i}{H_{n}}=\frac{1}{iH_{n}}.

But the
H_{n}
’s cancel out when we compute

\displaystyle\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{p_{j}}{p_{i}+p_{j}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{1/j}{1/i+1/j}

\displaystyle=\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{i}{i+j}.

We can use this to get an upper bound on the expected
search cost

\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\E\left[{D_{i}}\right]

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{iH_{n}}\left(1+\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{i}{i+j}\right)

\displaystyle<1+\frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{i+j}

\displaystyle<1+\frac{1}{H_{n}}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}\frac{k-1}{k}

\displaystyle<1+\frac{1}{H_{n}}\cdot 2n

\displaystyle=O(n/\log n).

To get a matching lower bound, notice that the best
possible ordering places each
i
at position
i
,
giving an expected search cost of exactly
\sum_{i}\frac{1}{iH_{n}}\cdot i=n/H_{n}=\Omega(n/\log n)
.
Since whatever random ordering we end up with is at
least this bad, this gives us the
\Theta(n/\log n)
bound we are looking for.

A.4
Assignment 4, due Thursday 2024-03-28 at 23:59

A.4.1
Nearly orthogonal vectors

Given two vectors
x
and
y
, the angle
\theta_{xy}
between them can be
computed by the formula
\theta_{xy}=\cos^{-1}\frac{x\cdot y}{\lVert x\rVert\lVert y\rVert}
. If
x
and
y
are orthogonal, then
x\cdot y=0
, and

\theta_{xy}=\pi/2
. Let’s call two vectors
x
and
y

nearly
orthogonal
to within
\epsilon
if
\pi/2-\epsilon\leq\theta_{xy}\leq\pi/2+\epsilon
.

Given an
n\times n
matrix
A
, we can find all the pairs of rows

A_{i},A_{j}
that are nearly orthogonal by computing
\theta_{A_{i},A_{j}}

for each pair and comparing it to
\pi/2\pm\epsilon
. Unfortunately, this
takes
\Theta(n^{3})
time if done in the obvious way. So let’s allow a
randomized approximation algorithm.

Claim: For any fixed
\epsilon
with
0<\epsilon\leq\pi/4
, there is a randomized algorithm that
takes as input an
n\times n
matrix
A
and an error parameter
\delta>0
,
and returns in time
O(n^{2}\log^{c}n\log^{c}(1/\delta))
, for some
constant
c
, a list of nearly-orthogonal
pairs of rows of
A
, such that with probability at least
1-\delta
,
this list includes every pair of rows
that are nearly orthogonal to within
\epsilon
,
and only pairs of rows that are nearly orthogonal to within
2\epsilon
.

Prove this claim.

Solution

This is a job for the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma
(distributional version).

First normalize the rows of
A
so that each
\lVert A_{i}\rVert=1
.
This takes
O(n^{2})
time and doesn’t affect the angles between
rows.

Next, observe for any unit vectors
x
and
y
,
\lVert x-y\rVert_{2}

is an increasing function of
\theta=\theta_{xy}
. We don’t actually
need anything more than this, but if we want to we can compute
the distance exactly by constructing an isosceles triangle with
x

and
y
as the unit edges and chopping it in half: this gives

\lVert x-y\rVert_{2}=2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}
. So if
\theta\leq\epsilon
,

\lVert x-y\rVert_{2}\leq 2\sin\frac{\epsilon}{2}
, and if
\theta\geq 2\epsilon
,

\lVert x-y\rVert_{2}>2\sin\epsilon
.

Pick a threshold halfway between these two bounds.
By choosing a small enough error term in
Lemma
8.1.2
, we can
guarantee that any pair
x,y
that is nearly orthogonal to
within
\epsilon
has
\lVert f(x-y)\rVert_{2}
close enough to

\lVert x-y\rVert^{2}
to be within this threshold, and any pair

x,y
that is not nearly orthogonal to within
2\epsilon
doesn’t.
(We could calculate what the exact error bound we need for
this, but since it’s a constant, we don’t care.) If we set the
probability of exceeding the error bound for a single vector
to
\delta/\binom{n}{2}
, this gives a probability that

\lVert A_{i}-A-j\rVert^{2}
exceeds the relative error bound for any

i,j
of at most
\delta
. To obtain
\delta/\binom{n}{2}
probability
of error, we need
k=O(\log(\delta/n^{2}))=O(\log n+\log\delta)
.

So now we need to feed all of our rows to the
Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform whose existence is given in
the lemma and then check the threshold for each pair of rows
in the output. Expanding out the steps, we must:

1.

Compute an
n\times k
transform matrix
B
implementing

f
. This takes
O(nk)
time.

2.

Compute
AB
. This takes
O(n^{2}k)
time using
ordinary matrix multiplication.

3.

For each pair of rows
i
and
j
, compute

\lVert(AB)_{i}-(AB)_{j}\rVert^{2}
and check it against the
thresholds. This takes
O(k)
time per pair of rows
for
O(n^{2}k)
time total.

Adding up all of these costs gives
O(n^{2}k)=O(n(\log n+\log(1/\delta)))
time, which is within the claimed bounds.

A.4.2
Boosting a random walk

Suppose you are made to participate in a fair
\pm 1
random walk,
starting with
X_{0}=k\leq n/2
, that ends if
X_{t}\geq n
or
X_{t}\leq 0
. The
twist is that once and only once during the walk only you can push a
“boost” button that replaces the normal transition rule
X_{t+1}=X_{t}\pm 1
with a rule that doubles the current value:
X_{t+1}=2X_{t}
.
Naturally, your choice to use your boost can’t depend on knowledge
of the future: when choosing to set
X_{t+1}=2X_{t}
, you only
know the outcomes
X_{1},\dots,X_{t}
.

1.

Suppose that your goal is to maximize the probability
that you reach a state
X_{t}\geq n
before you reach
X_{t}=0
. What
strategy should you use and what probability of reaching

X_{t}\geq n
(as a function of
k
and
n
) does it give you?

2.

Suppose instead that you want to
minimize
the
probability that you reach a state
X_{t}\geq n
before you
reach reach
0
, but you want to do this in a way that
always uses the boost before you reach
X_{t}\geq n
or
X_{t}=0
,
so that suspicious onlookers won’t think you
aren’t trying. Now what strategy should you use, and what
probability of reaching
X_{t}\geq n
does it give you?

Solution

Let’s formalize things a bit. Let
\left\{{\Delta_{t}}\right\}
be the set of
independent fair
\pm 1
increments, so that
X_{t+1}=X_{t}+\Delta_{t+1}
if we don’t use the boost. Then we can let
\mathcal{F}_{t}=\left\langle{\Delta_{1},\dots,\Delta_{t}}\right\rangle
and make the time
\sigma
at which we use
the boost a stopping time with respect to
\left\{{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right\}
. This
makes
[\sigma\leq t]
measurable
\mathcal{F}_{t}
for each
t
and gives

\E\left[{\Delta_{t+1}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right]=0
.

We can now write the transition rule compactly as

\displaystyle X_{t+1}

\displaystyle=2^{[\sigma=t]}X_{t}+[\sigma\neq t]\Delta_{t+1},

where
[A]
denotes the indicator variable for the event
A
.

Because of the boost,
\left\{{X_{t}}\right\}
is not a martingale with
respect to
\left\{{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right\}
, but we can define a process that is.

Let
Y_{t}=2^{[\sigma\geq t]}X_{t}
. The idea is that the first factor
represents whether we still have a boost available to use or
not.

Note that
[\sigma\geq t]
starts at
1
when
t=0
and drops to

0
when we use the boost. We can write this as
[\sigma\geq t+1]=[\sigma\geq t]-[\sigma=t]
.
This lets us compute

\displaystyle\E\left[{Y_{t+1}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right]

\displaystyle=\E\left[{2^{[\sigma\geq t+1]}X_{t+1}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right]

\displaystyle=\E\left[{2^{[\sigma\geq t+1]}\left(2^{[\sigma=t]}X_{t}+[\sigma\neq t]\Delta_{t+1}\right)}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right]

\displaystyle=2^{[\sigma\geq t]-[\sigma=t]}\cdot 2^{[\sigma=t]}X_{t}+2^{[\sigma\geq t+1]}[\sigma\neq t]\E\left[{\Delta_{t+1}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right]

\displaystyle=2^{[\sigma\geq t]}X_{t}

\displaystyle=Y_{t}.

So
\left\{{Y_{t}}\right\}
is a martingale with respect to
\left\{{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right\}
.

(Here we could pull
X_{t}
,
2^{\sigma\geq t}
,
2^{\sigma\geq t+1}=2^{[\sigma>t]}
, and
[\sigma\neq t]
out of
the conditional expectation because all these variables are
measurable
\mathcal{F}_{t}
.)

Let
\tau=\min\left\{{t}\;\middle|\;{X_{t}\geq n\vee X_{t}=0}\right\}
. Then
\tau
is
finite with probability
1
(if nothing else, we eventually
take
n
positive steps in a row), and
\left\lvert Y_{i}\right\rvert\leq 2n
, so
we can apply the finite probability / bounded range version of
the Optional Stopping Theorem to get

\displaystyle\E\left[{Y_{0}}\right]

\displaystyle=\E\left[{Y_{\tau}}\right]

\displaystyle=\E\left[{Y_{\tau}}\;\middle|\;{X_{\tau}\geq n}\right]\Pr\left[{X_{\tau}\geq n}\right]+\E\left[{Y_{\tau}}\;\middle|\;{X_{\tau}=0}\right]\Pr\left[{X_{\tau}=0}\right]

\displaystyle=\E\left[{Y_{\tau}}\;\middle|\;{X_{\tau}\geq n}\right]\Pr\left[{X_{\tau}\geq n}\right].

Since we know
\E\left[{Y_{0}}\right]=2k
, this gives

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{X_{\tau}\geq n}\right]

\displaystyle=\frac{2k}{\E\left[{Y_{\tau}}\;\middle|\;{X_{\tau}\geq n}\right]}.

(A.4.1)

We should thus try to minimize or maximize
\E\left[{Y_{\tau}}\;\middle|\;{X_{\tau}\geq n}\right]

depending on whether we want to maximize or minimize

\Pr\left[{X_{\tau}\geq n}\right]
.

1.

To minimize
\E\left[{Y_{t}}\;\middle|\;{X_{\tau}\geq n}\right]
, observe that the
smallest possible value for
Y_{\tau}
given
X_{\tau}\geq n

is
Y_{\tau}=X_{\tau}=n
. We can get this by using the boost
immediately (
\sigma=0
). Then we have a standard fair
random walk starting from
X_{1}=2k
, which hits
n

before
0
with probability exactly
\frac{2k}{n}
.

This is not necessarily the only good strategy, since any
strategy that guarantees
\sigma<\tau
and
X_{\sigma}\leq n/2
will
also get
\frac{2k}{n}
, but
(
A.4.1
) tells us
that no strategy can do better.

2.

To maximize
\E\left[{Y_{\tau}}\;\middle|\;{X_{\tau}\geq n}\right]
subject to the
requirement that we must use the boost, we want

\E\left[{X_{\tau}}\;\middle|\;{X_{\tau}\geq n}\right]
to be as large as possible. The
best we can hope to get is
X_{\tau}=2(n-1)
, by
using the boost on when
X_{t}=n-1
. But what if we
don’t reach
n-1
and are forced to use the boost
anyway?

Analyzing this using the
Y_{t}
martingale turns out to
be tricky, and an easier approach is just to guess the
worst strategy and show that it is in fact the worst. Since we
must use the boost before
\tau
, we are forced to use
the boost if we reach
1
or
n-1
, since otherwise
there is a possibility the process finishes before we
use it. Let’s suppose we adopt a maximum-delay
strategy and set
\sigma=\min\left\{{t}\;\middle|\;{t\in\left\{{1,n-1}\right\}}\right\}
.

Starting from any position
x
, this
\sigma
gives

\Pr\left[{X_{\tau}=n}\right]
of
2/n
if we reach
1
first and
1
if we
reach
n-1
first. Which we reach first is just the
probability of hitting on or the other absorbing
barrier in a simple random walk in
[1,n-1]
.
So we can compute

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{X_{\tau}=n}\;\middle|\;{X_{t}=x,t<\tau}\right]

\displaystyle=\frac{x-1}{n-2}\cdot 1+\left(1-\frac{x-1}{n-2}\right)\cdot\frac{2}{n}

\displaystyle=\frac{x-1}{n-2}\left(1-\frac{2}{n}\right)+\frac{2}{n}

\displaystyle=\frac{x-1}{n-2}\left(\frac{n-2}{n}\right)+\frac{2}{n}

\displaystyle=\frac{x-1}{n}+\frac{2}{n}

\displaystyle=\frac{x+1}{n}.

In particular, starting at
X_{0}=k
gives a
probability of hitting the upper barrier of

\frac{k+1}{n}
.

Now suppose we consider some other strategy
\sigma^{\prime}
.
Like
\sigma
,
\sigma^{\prime}
must use the boost at
X_{t}=1
or
X_{t}=n-1
.
If
X_{\sigma^{\prime}}=x
for some
x
with
1<x<n-1
, then

\Pr\left[{X_{\tau}\geq n}\;\middle|\;{X_{\sigma}=x}\right]=\frac{2x}{n}>\frac{x+1}{n}
since
x>1
. So any other
\sigma^{\prime}

gives a higher probability of
X_{\tau}\geq n
.

A.5
Assignment 5, due Thursday 2024-04-11 at 23:59

A.5.1
Relaxation time for Metropolis-Hastings

Suppose we have a lazy irreducible reversible Markov chain on
n

states with
transition probabilities
p_{ij}
, uniform stationary distribution

\pi_{i}=1/n
, and relaxation time
\tau_{2}
. Fix some function
f
with

1\leq f(x)\leq r
for all states
x
and apply Metropolis-Hastings to get
a new Markov chain with transition probabilities
p^{\prime}_{ij}=p_{ij}\min\left(1,f(j)/f(i)\right)
and stationary distribution
\pi^{\prime}_{i}\propto f(i)
. Let
\tau^{\prime}_{2}
be the relaxation time of this new
chain.

Prove or disprove: Under these assumptions, there is an
upper bound on
\tau^{\prime}_{2}
that is
polynomial in
\tau_{2}
and
r
.

Solution

We will prove this by showing that
\pi^{\prime}_{u}
and
p^{\prime}_{uv}
are
both bounded relative to their unmodified versions by
polynomial functions of
r
, then show this leads to at most
polynomial blowup
going from
\tau_{2}
to the
conductance
\Phi
of the original chain to the conductance
\Phi^{\prime}

of the modified chain and finally to
\tau^{\prime}_{2}
.

Let
n
be the number of states.
For
\pi^{\prime}_{u}
, we have

\displaystyle\pi^{\prime}_{u}

\displaystyle=\frac{f(u)}{\sum_{v}f(v)}\geq\frac{1}{(n-1)r+1}>\frac{1}{nr}=\frac{1}{r}\pi_{u}

and in the other direction

\displaystyle\pi^{\prime}_{u}

\displaystyle=\frac{f(u)}{\sum_{v}f(v)}\leq\frac{r}{(n-1)+r}<\frac{r}{n}=r\pi_{u}.

For
p^{\prime}_{uv}=p_{uv}\min\left(1,f(v)/f(u)\right)
, we
get
\frac{1}{r}p_{uv}\leq p^{\prime}_{uv}\leq p_{uv}
.

So now let’s look at some set of states
S
and try to bound

\Phi^{\prime}(S)
.

\displaystyle\Phi^{\prime}(S)

\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{u\in S,u\not\in S}\pi^{\prime}_{u}p^{\prime}_{uv}}{\pi^{\prime}(S)}

\displaystyle>\frac{\sum_{u\in S,u\not\in S}\frac{1}{r}\pi_{u}\cdot\frac{1}{r}p_{uv}}{r\pi(S)}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{r^{3}}\frac{\sum_{u\in S,u\not\in S}\pi_{u}p_{uv}}{\pi(S)}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{r^{3}}\Phi(S).

(A.5.1)

We’d like to use this to bound
\Phi^{\prime}=\min_{0<\pi^{\prime}(S)\leq 1/2}\Phi^{\prime}(S)
in terms of
r
and
\Phi=\min_{0<\pi(S)\leq 1/2}\Phi(S)
,
but there is a complication: there may be sets
S
with
\pi^{\prime}(S)\leq 1/2
but
\pi(S)>1/2
that are included in the computation
of
\Phi^{\prime}
but not
\Phi
. For these sets we will need to take
advantage of reversibility.

Suppose
\pi^{\prime}(S)\leq 1/2
,
\pi(S)>1/2
. Let
T=\overline{S}
.
Then
\pi(T)=1-\pi(S)<1/2
, so
\Phi(T)\leq\Phi
.
Now we can argue

\displaystyle\Phi^{\prime}(S)

\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{u\in S,v\in T}\pi^{\prime}_{u}p^{\prime}_{uv}}{\pi^{\prime}(S)}

\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{v\in T,u\in S}\pi^{\prime}_{v}p^{\prime}_{vu}}{\pi^{\prime}(S)}

\displaystyle=\Phi^{\prime}(T)\frac{\pi^{\prime}(T)}{\pi^{\prime}(S)}.

\displaystyle>\frac{1}{r^{3}}\Phi(T)\frac{\pi^{\prime}(T)}{\pi^{\prime}(S)}.

\displaystyle>\frac{1}{r^{3}}\Phi\cdot\frac{1/2}{1/2}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{r^{3}}\Phi.

(A.5.2)

So given
S
with
0<\pi^{\prime}(S)\leq 1/2
,
(
A.5.1
) shows
\Phi^{\prime}(S)\geq r^{-3}\Phi
when
\pi(S)\leq 1/2
and
(
A.5.2
) shows

\Phi^{\prime}(S)\geq r^{-3}\Phi
when
\pi(S)>1/2
. In either case we get
\Phi^{\prime}=\min_{0<\pi^{\prime}(S)\leq 1/2}\Phi^{\prime}(S)\geq r^{-3}\Phi
.

From (
10.6.4
), we have
\frac{1}{2\Phi}\leq\tau_{2}
, which gives
\Phi\geq\frac{1}{2\tau_{2}}
. But then we can apply
the other direction of (
10.6.4
) to
get

\displaystyle\tau^{\prime}_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{2}{(\Phi^{\prime})^{2}}<\frac{2}{(r^{-3}\Phi)^{2}}\leq\frac{2r^{6}}{(1/(2\tau_{2}))^{2}}=8r^{6}\tau_{2}^{2},

which is polynomial in
\tau_{2}
and
r
.

Though it doesn’t affect the solution to the problem, it is
probably worth noting here that there may be a much more efficient
way to sample proportional to
f
, which is to sample a point
uniformly (in time
O(\tau_{2}\log n/\epsilon)
) and then apply rejection
sampling to adjust the probabilities. This yields a sample in

O(r\tau_{2}\log n/\epsilon)
in the worst case where
f
is
1
for most
points and so we only return a sample with probability
1/r
. So
we may wish to reserve Metropolis-Hastings for situations where

f
has a much larger range (making rejection sampling too costly)
and we can show a tighter bound on convergence time in some other
way.

A.5.2
A constrained random walk

Let’s imagine we want to sample
n
-bit strings with no
consecutive pairs of
ones. So
00101
is acceptable but
01101
is not.

It’s possible to do this efficiently and exactly by taking
advantage of the connection of these strings to Fibonacci numbers,
but for some unexplained reason we decide to do this using Markov
Chain Monte Carlo instead. Given an initial string
x
,
pick an index
i
and bit
b
uniformly at random, and set
x_{i}

to
b
unless this would produce two consecutive ones. It is not
hard to show that this gives an irreducible aperiodic Markov chain
that converges to a uniform stationary distribution.

Show that this chain has the rapid mixing property, which means
that

t_{\mix}(\epsilon)
is polylogarithmic in the number of states
N
and
the total variation distance bound
\epsilon
.

Solution

First observe that the number of possible states
N
is at least

2^{\lceil n/2\rceil}
, the number of strings with zeros in all
odd-numbered positions.
2
2

2

This is a rather crude
estimate that is convenient mostly because itit is instantly
recognizable as exponential in
n
. As hinted at in the problem
statement, we can compute
N
exactly using Fibonacci
numbers. Each acceptable string of length
2
or more either
starts with
0

followed by an acceptable string of length
n-1
, or starts
with
10
followed by an acceptable string of length
n-2
.
This gives a recurrence
N(n)=N(n-1)+N(n-2
with
N(0)=1
and
N(1)=2
. This is exactly the recurrence for
Fibonacci numbers shifted so that
N(n)=F_{n+2}
, which is
not surprising when we recall that Pingala
invented Fibonacci numbers precisely to count sequences of
syllables of length
1
or
2
adding up to a given total.
So if we can get a mixing time that is
polynomial in
n
, it will be polylogarithmic in
n
.

Coupling and canonical paths are both options for showing such a
bound.

One possible coupling is to apply the same update rule to both
the
X
and
Y
processes: Pick an index
i
and a bit
i
and
update each of
X_{i}
and
Y_{i}
to equal
b
if permitted by
the no consecutive ones rule. We can then track how the
Hamming distance between
X
and
Y
evolves over time.

Let
S^{t}=\left\{{i}\;\middle|\;{X^{t}_{i}\neq Y^{t}_{i}}\right\}
and let
H^{t}=\left\lvert S^{t}\right\rvert
. Then
H^{t}
can
change in two ways:

•

If we pick some
i\in S
, then
H
always drops
by
1
if
b=0
, and drops by
1
if
b=1
and neither

i-1
nor
i+1
is in
S
.

•

If we pick some
i\not\in S
, then
H
stays the same if

i-1
and
i+1
are both not in
S
and goes up by
1

if either is in
S
.

Partition
S
into segments
S_{1},\dots,S_{k}
where each
S_{k}

is a maximal sequence of consecutive indices.

If
\lvert S_{i}\rvert=1
, then the index in
S_{i}
contributes a

\frac{1}{n}
chance of lowering
H
, and the adjacent indices
together contribute at most a
\frac{1}{n}
chance of increasing
H
.

If
\lvert S_{i}\rvert=k>1
, then each index in
S_{i}
contributes a

\frac{1}{2n}
chance of lowering
H
, for a total of

\frac{k}{2n}\geq\frac{1}{n}
, and the adjacent indices
together contribute at most a
\frac{1}{n}
chance of increasing
H
.

In either case we have
\E\left[{H^{t+1}}\;\middle|\;{X^{t},Y^{t}}\right]\leq H^{t}
,
with at least a
\frac{2}{n}
chance that
H
changes if
H>0
.
We also have that
H
never exceeds
n
and never changes
once it reaches
0
. So we can bound
H
by a fair random walk

H^{\prime}
with a reflecting barrier at
n
and absorbing barrier at

0
, that only takes a step when
H
does. This shows that
H

reaches
0
in
O(n^{3})
steps on average.

For canonical paths,
given two states
x
and
y
that differ in
k
places, we’ll
define a path
\gamma_{xy}
of length
k
that fixes these bits one
at a time. We can’t do strict left-to-right bit fixing,
because this may create an intermediate state that has two
consecutive ones. But we can adjust the order a little to get
around this: at each step, change the leftmost unfixed bit
that can be changed without violating the no-consecutive ones
rule.

A step in such a path changes some string of the form

y_{1}\dots y_{\ell}rsx_{\ell+3}\dots x_{n}

to

y_{1}\dots y_{\ell}r^{\prime}s^{\prime}x_{\ell+3}\dots x_{n}
,
where the
rs\rightarrow r^{\prime}s^{\prime}
change is one of
00\rightarrow 10
,
01\rightarrow 00
, or

10\rightarrow 00
. To reconstruct
x
and
y
from this information,
it is enough to provide
\ell
(
n-2
choices), a string
x_{1}\dots x_{\ell+1}0y_{\ell+3}\dots y_{n}
with no consecutive ones (
<N
choices), and the
values of
x_{\ell+2}
and
y_{\ell+2}
(4 choices).
This gives
<4nN
paths crossing each edge, so
the congestion
\rho
is

\displaystyle\max_{uv\in E}\frac{1}{\pi_{u}p_{uv}}\sum_{\gamma_{xy}\ni uv}\pi_{x}\pi_{y}

\displaystyle<\frac{1}{N^{-1}(1/(2n))}\cdot 4nN\cdot N^{-2}=8n^{2}.

We thus get
\tau_{2}\leq 8\rho^{2}=O(n^{4})
, with a hideous constant
swept behind the big
O
for decency’s sake. This again is
polylogarithmic in
N
, so we’re done.

A.6
Assignment 6, due Thursday 2024-04-25 at 23:59

A.6.1
The power of intransigence

Let
G
be a connected graph on
n
vertices labeled
1,\dots,n
,
and imagine each vertex
v
in
G
represents a person who has an
opinion
X^{t}_{v}\in\left\{{0,1}\right\}
at each time
t
. This opinion is
initially arbitrary, but may evolve over time to match the
opinions of
v
’s neighbors.

Specifically, at each step, we pick one of the
m
edges in the
graph uniformly at
random, and then choose a random orientation of that edge to get
an ordered pair of
adjacent vertices
ij
, with each possible pair chosen with
probability
\frac{1}{2m}
. Most of the time, this results in
j

adopting
i
’s opinion, so that
X^{t+1}_{j}=X^{t}_{i}
, while

X^{t+1}_{k}=X^{t}_{k}
for all
k\neq j
.

But not if
j=1
. Vertex
1
is stubborn: headstrong, willful,
convinced in its bones that it is right, holding
a graduate degree in obstinacy in one hand and a thesaurus opened
to “stubborn” in the other to back up its
unyielding pig-headed beliefs.
If we are unlucky enough to pick
j=1
, then nothing changes and
X^{t+1}=X^{t}
.

Running this process long enough will eventually converge to a
state where every other vertex gives up and agrees with vertex
1
.
There is even a constant
c
such that it reaches this state in

\Theta(n^{c})
steps on average with the worst possible
G
and the
worst possible
X^{0}
.

Find
c
, and prove that this bound holds.

Solution

We’ll show
c=4
.

For the lower bound, we just need one bad family of graphs
and starting configurations that gives
\Omega(n^{4})
expected
convergence time. One choice is a lollipop graph, consisting
of a handle that is a path of
n/2
vertices and a sucker that
is
K_{n/2}
, plus an edge linking one end of the path to one
vertex in the clique.

Let’s make the stubborn node be a member of the clique with
initial value
0
, and start in a configuration where the
most distant
n/4
nodes in the path have
1
and everybody
else has
0
. Let
X^{t}_{i}
be the value of node
i
at time
t

and let
Z_{t}=\sum_{i}X^{t}
. Then as long as all the clique nodes
have
X^{t}_{i}=0
and some path node has
X^{t}_{i}=1
, we have a
configuration where the
1
nodes are exactly the
Z_{t}
most
distant nodes on the path. So
Z^{t+1}=Z_{t}
only if we pick
the unique
0-1
edge, and we have
Z^{t+1}=Z_{t}\pm 1
with
probability
\frac{1}{2m}
each.

This give an unbiased random walk that takes steps with
probability
\frac{1}{m}
. It takes
(n/4)^{2}
steps for this
to reach
Z_{t}=0
or
Z_{t}=n/2
, which is a lower bound on
the time for the process as a whole to converge. The waiting
time for each random walk step is
m
, so the total expected
time to reach
Z_{t}=0
or
Z_{t}=n/2
is
m(n/4)^{2}
by Wald’s
Equation. The clique makes
m=\Omega(n^{2})
, so the expected time
to converge is
\Omega(n^{4})
.

In the other direction, we will show that any graph reaches
an all-equal state from any initial state in time
O(n^{4})
.
For this argument it’s convenient to assume that the stubborn
node starts with
1
, so we finish when
Z_{t}=n
.

Fix some configuration
X^{t}
, and let
\ell
be the number of

0-1
edges in
X^{t}
. Let
\mathcal{F}_{t}=\left\langle{X^{0},X^{1},\dots,X^{t}}\right\rangle
be
the
\sigma
-algebra generated by the trajectory of the system up
until time
t
.
Then
\Pr\left[{Z^{t+1}-Z_{t}=1}\right]{\mathcal{F}_{t}}=\frac{\ell}{2m}
and

\Pr\left[{Z^{t+1}-Z_{t}=-1}\right]{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\leq\frac{\ell}{2m}
(because
edges incident to the stubborn vertex don’t contribute). The
rest of the time
Z^{t+1}=Z_{t}
.

This gives a
\pm 1
random walk that may be biased toward
+1

and that takes steps only some of the time. There are two
mostly equivalent ways to bound the convergence time of this
process: one uses an explicit potential function, and the
other reduces to known results about random walks via a
coupling argument. We’ll describe both below, since either
gives a reasonable solution to this part of the problem.

Potential function argument

Consider the function
Z_{t}^{2}
.
The expected change in this quantity is

\displaystyle\E\left[{Z_{t+1}^{2}-Z_{t}^{2}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right]

\displaystyle\geq(2Z_{t}+1)\Pr\left[{Z_{t+1}=Z_{t}+1}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}+t}\right]

\displaystyle\quad+(-2Z_{t}+1)\Pr\left[{Z_{t+1}=Z_{t}-1}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}+t}\right]

\displaystyle\geq(2Z_{t}+1)\frac{\ell}{2m}+(-2Z_{t}+1)\frac{\ell}{2m}

\displaystyle=\frac{\ell}{m}

\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{m}.

(The second step uses
Z_{t}\geq 1
, as enforced by the stubborn
vertex.)

If we define
Y_{t}=Z_{t}^{2}-\frac{t}{m}
, then
Y_{t}
is a
submartingale, since the expected increase in
Z_{t}^{2}
always pays
for the increase in
\frac{t}{m}
.
So at any stopping time
\tau
that satisfies the conditions of
the Optional Stopping Theorem for
\left\{{Y_{t}}\right\}
,
\E\left[{Y_{\tau}}\right]\geq\E\left[{Y_{0}}\right]
.

Let
\tau
be the first time at which
Z_{\tau}=n
.
Then
Y_{\tau}=Z_{\tau}^{2}-\frac{\tau}{m}=n^{2}-\frac{\tau}{m}
.
For
t\leq\tau
,
Y_{t}
and
\tau
satisfy the bounded increments and
finite expected time conditions, because
Y_{t}
can’t change by
more than
2n+\frac{1}{m}
in this range and
\tau
has finite
expectation by the usual argument for Markov chain hitting
times. So
\E\left[{Y_{\tau}}\right]=n^{2}-\frac{1}{m}\E\left[{\tau}\right]\geq Y_{0}=Z_{0}^{2}\geq 0
. Solve to get
\E\left[{\tau}\right]\leq mn^{2}=O(n^{4})
.

Coupling argument

An alternative argument couples
Z^{t}
with an unbiased random
walk
W_{t}
with a reflecting barrier at
0
, that takes steps
at random times
T_{1},T_{2},\dots
, where
\E\left[{T_{i+1}-T_{i}}\right]\leq m
. The idea is to move
W_{t}
only when we pick a
0-1
edge
n the
X^{t}
process, and argue that we can always keep
Z_{t}\geq W_{t}
by incrementing
W_{t}
whenever we increment
Z_{t}
and
decrementing
W_{t}
even if
Z_{t}
doesn’t go down because of
stubbornness. So when
W_{t}
reaches
n
after at most
n^{2}m

expected steps (Wald’s Equation again!),
Z_{t}
must already
have reached
n
.

(This is pretty much the same argument as the potential
function argument, except that we hide the potential function inside
the known
n^{2}
bound for the unbiased random walk. I think
the coupling argument is more satisfying in some ways because
it more intuitively describes what the
Z_{t}
process is doing.
However, at least as written above, it skips over justifying some details
that don’t come up with the potential function, so there is
also more room for error.)

A.6.2
Almost Markov

Let
G
be a
d
-regular graph on
n
vertices. Assign a label

\ell(v)\in\left\{{0,1}\right\}
to each vertex. Let
V_{0}V_{1}V_{2}\dots
be a
random walk on
G
starting at some initial fixed vertex
v_{0}
,
where each
V_{t+1}
is chosen uniformly among the
d
neighbors
of
V_{t}
, and let
\ell(V_{0}),\ell(V_{1}),\ell(V_{2}),\dots
be the
sequence of vertex labels observed during this random walk.

Call the sequence
\ell(V_{0}),\ell(V_{1}),\ell(V_{2}),\dots

almost Markov
with error
\epsilon
if, for all
t\geq 0
,

1/2-\epsilon\leq\E\left[{\ell(V_{t+1})}\;\middle|\;{\ell(V_{0}),\dots,\ell(V_{t})}\right]\leq 1/2+\epsilon
.

Show that, for any fixed
\epsilon>0
, there is some minimum degree

d_{\epsilon}
, such that for any
d
-regular graph
G
on
n
vertices, it
is possible to compute a labeling on
G
in expected time
polynomial in
n
and
d
, such that a random walk on
G
starting
from any vertex produces a sequence of labels

\ell(V_{0}),\ell(V_{1}),\ell(V_{2}),\dots
that is
almost Markov with error
\epsilon
.

Solution

Suppose we label each vertex independently and uniformly at
random. For each vertex
v
, let
N(v)
be the set of all
nodes adjacent to
v
, let
L_{v}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{u\in N(v)}\ell(v)
be the probability that taking a step starting at V
lands on a node labeled with a 1, and let

A_{v}
be the event
\left\lvert L_{v}-1/2\right\rvert>\epsilon
.

Observe that if none of the events
A_{v}
occurs,
we get the almost-Markov property because the bound on

\E\left[{\ell(V_{t+1}}\right]
will hold conditioned on any previous vertex
V_{t}
.
We will use the Lovász Local Lemma to show that a labeling
exists that makes none of these occur, and then use
Moser-Tardos to find one.

With a bit of tinkering, we can write
L_{v}-1/2
as the sum of
d

independent
\pm\frac{1}{2d}
random variables, so
Hoeffding’s inequality says

\displaystyle p

\displaystyle=\Pr\left[{A_{v}}\right]\leq\Pr\left[{\lvert L_{v}-1/2\rvert\geq\epsilon}\right]\leq 2e^{-\epsilon^{2}/2d(1/d^{2})}=2e^{-d\epsilon^{2}}.

Let
\Gamma(A_{v})=\left\{{A_{u}}\;\middle|\;{d(v,u)=2}\right\}
. Then
A_{v}
is independent of
any event
A_{u}\not\in\Gamma(A_{v})\cup\left\{{A_{v}}\right\}
, because only events in this
set depend on vertices that are adjacent to
v
, which are the
only ones that affect
A_{v}
. Because the graph is
d
-regular, there
are at most
d(d-1)
vertices at distance 2 from
v
, and thus at
most
d(d-1)
events in
\Gamma(A_{v})
.

The Lovász Local Lemma applies if
ep(d(d-1)+1)<1
, which holds
if
e\cdot 2e^{-d\epsilon^{2}}\cdot(d(d-1)+1)<1
. For any fixed
\epsilon
, the
expression on the left goes to zero in the limit as
d
increases, so there
exists some value
d_{\epsilon}
such that the bound holds for all
d\geq d_{\epsilon}
. If the bound does hold, LLL says that there exists a
labeling that makes none of the
A_{v}
happen.

Using the Moser-Tardos algorithm
[
MT10
]
, we can
find such a labeling in
\frac{n}{d(d-1)}
resamplings on
average.
The efficient way to manage the resamplings is to compute all
the
L_{v}
values initially in
O(nd)
time, and then pay

O(d^{2})
time for each resampling to update the values and
check any that have changed.
If we do this, the initial setup cost dominates on average, giving an
overall expected
O(nd)
total time, which is about the best
we could reasonably hope for given the size of the input, and
which is polynomial in
n
and
d
as required.

B.1
Assignment 1, due Thursday 2023-02-16 at 23:59

B.1.1
Hashing without counting

Suppose we are building a hash table with separate chaining, which
is implemented as an array of

m
positions
A[0],A[1],\dots,A[m-1]
,
each of which may hold zero or more elements in some
secondary data structure like a variable-length array or linked
list (see §
7.1
).
We’ll abstract away from the actual hash function and assume that
when a new element is inserted, its position is chosen
independently and uniformly at random.

Normally we would keep track of the number of elements
n

inserted into the table and grow the table by some constant factor
when the load factor
\alpha=n/m
gets too
big. But this is work and we are lazy. So instead we adopt the
following heuristic: grow the table as soon as some element is
inserted into position
0
. We’d like to make sure that this
heuristic doesn’t produce any bad outcomes, by looking at how
crowded the positions in the table are at the moment after this
element is placed in
A[0]
, just before expanding the table.

Specifically, for this configuration:

1.

Compute the exact expected load factor
\alpha=n/m
as a
function of
m
.

2.

Compute the best high-probability asymptotic bound you
can for the maximum number of elements in any table position as a function of
m
.
This means that you should find a function
f(m)
such
that for all
c>0
, the maximum number of elements is at
most
O(f(m))
with probability at least
1-m^{-c}
, where
the constant in the asymptotic bound may depend on
c
.

Solution

1.

Let
X
be the number of elements inserted into the
table. Then
X
counts the number of insertions up to
and including the first insertion to position
0
,
making it a geometric random variable with
parameter
p=1/m
(see
§
3.6.2
).
This gives
E[X]=m
.

The expected load factor is
E[X/m]=1
.

2.

Pick some
i\neq 0
, and let
X_{i}
be the number of
elements in position
i
.

Let’s calculate
\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k}\right]
.
If
k=0
, this is
1
.
Otherwise, when we insert the first element, there is a
1/n

chance it lands in position
i
, and a
1/n
chance it
lands in position
0
. The rest of the time it lands
in a position
j\not\in\left\{{0,i}\right\}
and has no effect on

X_{i}
.

So we have, for
k>0
,

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k}\right]

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k}\;\middle|\;{\text{insert $0$}}\right]

\displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{n}\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k}\;\middle|\;{\text{insert
$i$}}\right]

\displaystyle\quad+\frac{n-2}{n}\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k}\;\middle|\;{\text{insert
elsewhere}}\right]

which gives

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k}\right]

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k}\;\middle|\;{\text{insert $0$}}\right]

\displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{2}\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k}\;\middle|\;{\text{insert
$i$}}\right].

The first branch is
0
when
k>0
. For the second
branch, observe that
\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k}\;\middle|\;{\text{insert
$i$}}\right]=\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k-1}\right]
, since we already have one
element and now we are asking if we can get
k-1
more
using the same process that generates
X_{i}
. This
gives a recurrence:

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k}\right]

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1&k=0\\
\frac{1}{2}\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k-1}\right]&k>0\\
\end{cases}

which has the solution
\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k}\right]=2^{-k}
.

Now use the union bound to compute, for
k>1
:

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{\max X_{i}\geq k}\right]

\displaystyle=\Pr\left[{\exists i:X_{i}\geq k}\right]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\Pr\left[{X_{i}\geq k}\right]

\displaystyle=(n-1)2^{-k}.

Pick any
c>0
. Let
k=(c+1)\lg n
. Then

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{\max X_{i}\geq k}\right]

\displaystyle\leq(n-1)2^{-(c+1)\lg n}

\displaystyle=(n-1)n^{-c-1}

\displaystyle<n^{-c},

from which it follows that

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{\max X_{i}<(c+1)\lg n)}\right]

\displaystyle\geq 1-n^{-c}.

Since this makes
\max X_{i}=O(\log n)
with
probability
1-n^{-c}
for any fixed
c>0
, we get a
high-probability bound of
O(\log n)
.

Though this is not required by the problem, we can see
that it is not possible to do better than
O(\log m)

by looking at the distribution for a single bin. We
have
\Pr\left[{\max X_{i}\geq k}\right]\geq\Pr\left[{X_{1}\geq k}\right]=2^{-k}
,
so
\Pr\left[{\max X_{i}\geq c\lg m}\right]\geq m^{-c}
for any fixed

c
.

B.1.2
Permutation routing on an incomplete network

Suppose we have a network of
n=2d
senders and
n=2d

receivers, where each sender has outgoing links to exactly
d

distinct receivers. Other than this information,
the structure of the graph is unconstrained.

Let the senders be labeled
1\dots n
and let the receivers be
labeled
\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{n}
where
\pi
is a permutation of
1\dots n
chosen uniformly at random. Call a sender
i
“successful” if
there is a link from sender
i
to the receiver who is assigned
label
i
. Let
S
be the
number of successful senders. Then
S
is a random variable that
depends on the choice of
\pi
. (Figure
B.1

shows an example.)

1
2
3
4
4
1
3
2

1
2
3
4
3
1
2
4

Figure B.1:
An
incomplete network with
n=2d=4
. In the
left copy, the random permutation makes all four senders successful, giving
S=4
. In
the right copy, a different random permutation makes only sender

1
successful, giving
S=1
.

1.

What is the exact value of
\E\left[{S}\right]
as a function of
n
?

2.

What are the smallest and largest possible exact values of

\Variance\left[{S}\right]
as a function of
n
?

3.

Show that for any choice of
graph that satisfies the constraints above, at least

\Omega(n)
senders are successful with probability at least
1-o(1)
.

Solution

1.

Let
X_{i}
be the indicator variable for the event that
sender
i
is successful, so that
S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}
. Each
sender
i
is successful if and only if
i
is the label of one of
i
’s

d
neighbors. This occurs with probability
d/n=1/2
, so

\E\left[{X_{i}}\right]=1/2
and
\E\left[{S}\right]=n/2
.

2.

We have
\Variance\left[{S}\right]=\sum_{i}\Variance\left[{X_{i}}\right]+\sum_{i\neq j}\Covariance\left[{X_{i}},{Y_{i}}\right]
. Since the
X_{i}
are fair coin-flips we get

\Variance\left[{X_{i}}\right]=1/4
.

To bound
\Covariance\left[{X_{i}},{Y_{i}}\right]

let
\delta_{i}
and
\delta_{j}
be the neighborhoods of senders
i
and

j
, and let
c_{ij}=\left\lvert\delta_{i}\cap\delta_{j}\right\rvert
be the number of neighbors
these senders have in common. Then

\displaystyle\E\left[{X_{i}X_{j}}\right]

\displaystyle=\Pr\left[{i\in\delta_{i}\wedge j\in\delta_{j}}\right]

\displaystyle=\Pr\left[{i\in\delta_{i}\cap\delta_{j}}\right]\Pr\left[{j\in\delta_{j}}\;\middle|\;{i\in\delta_{i}\cap\delta_{j}}\right]

\displaystyle\quad+\Pr\left[{i\in\delta_{i}\setminus\delta_{j}}\right]\Pr\left[{j\in\delta_{j}}\;\middle|\;{i\setminus\delta_{i}\cap\delta_{j}}\right]

\displaystyle=\frac{c_{ij}}{n}\cdot\frac{d-1}{n-1}+\frac{d-c_{ij}}{n}\cdot\frac{d}{n-1}

\displaystyle=\frac{c_{ij}(d-1)+(d-c_{ij})d}{n(n-1)}

\displaystyle=\frac{c_{ij}d-c_{ij}+d^{2}-c_{ij}d}{n(n-1)}

\displaystyle=\frac{d^{2}-c_{ij}}{n(n-1)}.

This gives

\displaystyle\Covariance\left[{X_{i}},{X_{j}}\right]

\displaystyle=\E\left[{X_{i}X_{j}}\right]-\E\left[{X_{i}}\right]\E\left[{X_{j}}\right]

\displaystyle=\frac{d^{2}-c_{ij}}{n(n-1)}-\frac{d^{2}}{n^{2}}

\displaystyle=\frac{d^{2}n-c_{ij}n-d^{2}(n-1)}{n^{2}(n-1)}

\displaystyle=\frac{d^{2}-c_{ij}n}{n^{2}(n-1)}

\displaystyle=\frac{1/4-c_{ij}/n}{n-1}.

Summing over all
n(n-1)
pairs
i\neq j
gives

\displaystyle\Variance\left[{S}\right]

\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\Variance\left[{X_{i}}\right]+\sum_{i\neq j}\Covariance\left[{X_{i}},{X_{j}}\right]

\displaystyle=\frac{n}{4}+\frac{n}{4}-\sum_{i\neq j}\frac{c_{ij}}{n(n-1)}.

\displaystyle=\frac{n}{2}-\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}c_{ij}.

To minimize the variance, we want to make
\sum_{i\neq j}c_{ij}
as large as possible. We can do this by
routing all
n
senders to the same
d=n/2

receivers, giving
c_{ij}=n/2
for all
i\neq j
and
thus
\Variance\left[{S}\right]=0
.
This is not surprising because in this case, all and only
those senders whose ids appear among the
d
favored
receivers will be successful, making
S
a constant.

For the upper bound, we can get crude bound by
observing that
c_{ij}\geq 0
gives
\Variance\left[{S}\right]\leq n/2
. But
in general there is no graph that actually produces

c_{ij}=0
for all
i\neq j
. Instead, we need to look
at minimizing
\sum c_{ij}
subject to the constraint
that there are
nd
edges.

Let
e_{ijk}
be
1
if senders
i
and
j
share an edge to
receiver
k
and
0
otherwise.
Then
c_{ij}=\sum_{k}e_{ijk}
. But if we
write
d_{k}
for the degree of receiver
k
, we also
have that
\sum_{i\neq j}e_{ijk}=d_{k}(d_{k}-1)
, since
each ordered pair of distinct neighbors of
k
contributes one
nonzero
e_{ijk}
. It follows that

\displaystyle\sum_{i\neq j}c_{ij}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i\neq j}\sum_{k}e_{ijk}

\displaystyle=\sum_{k}d_{k}(d_{k}-1).

We have the constraint
\sum_{k}d_{k}=dn
; subject to this
constraint,
\sum_{k}d_{k}(d_{k}-1)
is minimized when all

d_{k}=d
. This can be achieved by routing each sender

i
to receivers
i,i+1,\dots i+(d-1)\pmod{n}
or
by routing all of the first
d
senders to all of
the first
d
receivers and similarly for the second

d
senders and receivers.

This gives

\displaystyle\Variance\left[{S}\right]

\displaystyle=\frac{n}{2}-\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}c_{ij}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{n}{2}-\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\cdot nd(d-1)

\displaystyle=\frac{n}{2}-\frac{d(d-1)}{n-1}

\displaystyle=\frac{n}{2}\left(1-\frac{n/2-1}{n-1}\right)

\displaystyle=\frac{n}{2}\cdot\frac{2n-2-n+2}{2(n-1}

\displaystyle=\frac{n^{2}}{4(n-1)}.

As a check, we can observe that when
n=2
, this
gives
\Variance\left[{S}\right]=1=n/2
, matching the crude bound
because in this case we can in fact guarantee no
overlap between senders’ neighborhoods.

3.

Since
\Variance\left[{S}\right]\leq n/2
, we can use Chebyshev’s inequality to compute

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{S\leq n/4}\right]

\displaystyle=\Pr\left[{S-\E\left[{S}\right]\leq-n/4}\right]

\displaystyle\leq\Pr\left[{\left\lvert S-\E\left[{S}\right]\right\rvert\geq n/4}\right]

\displaystyle\leq\frac{n/2}{(n/4)^{2}}

\displaystyle=1/n.

So our probability of getting at least
n/4=\Omega(n)
successful
senders is at least
1-1/n=1-o(1)
.

A tighter bound can be obtained using Azuma’s inequality with
an appropriate exposure martingale. Let
\mathcal{F}_{t}
be the

\sigma
-algebra generated by knowing which receiver is assigned
label
j
for all
j\leq t
. Let
Y_{t}=\E\left[{S}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right]
.

To apply Azuma’s inequality, we need a bound on

\left\lvert Y_{t+1}-Y_{T}\right\rvert
. Let’s look at
\E\left[{X_{i}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right]
and
how it changes with
t
.

(a)

If
i\leq t
, then the target for sender
i
is
already known, and
X_{i}
is either
0
or
1
. The
change
\E\left[{X_{i}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t+1}}\right]-\E\left[{X_{I}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t+1}}\right]

is exactly
0
in this case.

(b)

If
i=t+1
, then
\mathcal{F}_{t+1}
determines
x_{i}
.
Whatever the previous conditional expectation, the new
conditional expectation is either
0
or
1
. This
gives a change of at most
\pm 1
.

(c)

If
i>t+1
, then there are
n-t
possible places to
put label
i
, of which
d_{i}
are connected to
sender
i
for some
0\leq d_{i}\leq d
. The value of
d_{i}

depends on how many receivers connected to sender
i

have known labels in
\mathcal{F}_{t}
.

In this case we have

\displaystyle\E\left[{X_{i}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t+1}}\right]-\E\left[{X_{i}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right]

\displaystyle\leq\frac{d_{i}}{n-t-1}-\frac{d_{i}}{n-t}

\displaystyle=\frac{d_{i}}{(n-t)(n-t-1)}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{n-t}{(n-t)(n-t-1)}.

\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{n-t-1}.

In the other direction,

\displaystyle\E\left[{X_{i}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t+1}}\right]-\E\left[{X_{i}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right]

\displaystyle\geq\frac{d_{i}-1}{n-t-1}-\frac{d_{i}}{n-t}

\displaystyle=-\frac{n-t-d_{i}}{(n-t)(n-t-1)}

\displaystyle\geq-\frac{n-t}{(n-t)(n-t-1)},

\displaystyle\geq-\frac{1}{n-t-1}.

In either case the absolute value is bounded by

\frac{1}{n-t-1}
. There are
n-t-1
values of
i
in
this range, so the sum for all of them is at most
\pm 1
.

Combining the last two cases, we have

\left\lvert\E\left[{S}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t+1}}\right]-\E\left[{S}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right]\right\rvert\leq 2
.
So Azuma’s inequality gives
\Pr\left[{S-n/2\geq t}\right]\leq e^{-t^{2}/8n}

and similarly
\Pr\left[{S-n/2\leq t}\right]\leq e^{-t^{2}/8n}
. The constant
in the denominator could possibly be improved a bit with a
better analysis, but even as is we get that
S=n/2\pm\Theta(\sqrt{n\log n})
with high probability and
S\geq n/4=\Omega(n)

with all but exponentially small probability.

B.2
Assignment 2, due Thursday 2023-03-30 at 23:59

B.2.1
Some streaming data structures

Suppose you are given a stream
x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{2n}

of
2n
integer values in the range

0\dots n-1
. You are presented with these values one at a time.
Upon receiving each value, you may update a data structure of your
choosing that fits in
O(\log n)
bits of space. You have no other storage.

1.

Give an algorithm for
sampling a single value with probability proportional to
the number of times it occurs in the stream, returning
this value once all elements of the stream have been
processed.

For example, given a stream
1,0,1,2,1,1
, your algorithm
should return
0
or
2
with probability
1/6
each, and
return
1
with probability
2/3
.

2.

Give a Las Vegas algorithm that returns a value that occurs at least twice in the
stream with probability
\Omega(1)
. If it doesn’t succeed, it
should return
\bot
to indicate
failure. (This algorithm should never return a value that
occurs less than twice.)

In both cases, prove the correctness of your algorithm. You
may assume that
n
is known to the algorithm.

Solution

1.

There are two straightforward ways to do this using
O(\log n)
bits:

(a)

The easiest is to sample the position of the desired
element ahead of time, then count down until we hit
it. This requires
2n
possible states for the
countdown timer plus
n
possible states for the
stored value, for a total of
\lceil\lg 3n\rceil=O(\log n)
bits.

(b)

Alternatively, we could store a value while counting
how many values we’ve seen, and replace the stored
value with the
k
-th value with probability

1/k
.
1
1

1

This is a special case of a more
general algorithm known as

reservoir
sampling
, due to Vitter
[
Vit85
]
.

A straightforward induction argument shows that this
makes the stored value uniform across all the values
seen so far. We need
\lceil\lg 2n\rceil
bits for the
counter and
\lceil lgn\rceil
bits to store the current
value, but the total is still
O(\log n)
.

2.

For this part, the intuition is that we will sample a value
as we go, then record a winner if we happen to see it again.
How easy this is to analyze depends on which sampling
algorithm we use:

(a)

If we pick a particular position
i
and then sample

x_{i}
, we win as long as
x_{i}
is not the last
occurrence of this particular value in the sequence.
Since there are at most
n
positions that are the
last occurrence of a value, we have at least a
1-n/2n=1/2
chance of winning. This requires an extra bit
to record whether or not the sampled value appeared
again, for a total of
\lceil\lg 3n\rceil+1=O(\log n)

bits.

(b)

Alternatively, we could run the continuous sampling
algorithm above and fix the stored value if we see it again.
The analysis in this case is a bit more messy.
Here is one possible approach.

Consider the original sampling process, and
let
A_{i}
be the event that (a) there exists some
j>i
such that
x_{j}=x_{i}
, and (b) value
x_{i}
is
stored at time
i
and never overwritten.
There are at least
n
positions for which (a) holds,
and for each of these positions we have
\Pr\left[{A_{i}}\right]=1/2n
.

Unfortunately these events are not independent. But
for any
i
, we have that

\Pr\left[{\neg A_{i}}\;\middle|\;{\neg A_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge\neg A_{i-1}}\right]
is either

1
(if
A_{i}
never occurs) or at most
1-1/2n
(since
previous events
A_{j}
not occurring for
j<i
i
can only increase the likelihood of
A_{i}
occurring).
The latter case holds for at least
n
choices of
i
,
giving

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{\bigwedge\neg A_{i}}\right]

\displaystyle=\prod\Pr\left[{\neg A_{i}}\;\middle|\;{\neg A_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge\neg A_{i-1}}\right]

\displaystyle\leq(1-1/2n)^{n}

\displaystyle\leq e^{-1/2},

which is a constant strictly less than
1
. So with
constant probability, at least one event
A_{i}
occurs.
But then the algorithm observes a duplicate and
returns it.

B.2.2
A dense network

Suppose we construct a network as follows. Initially, we have
n_{0}=n
nodes, of which one is an inert base station with no incident edges.
We also have
m_{0}=m
edges between the
n-1
remaining nodes. At each step, we pick
one of the
n_{t}-1
non-base-station nodes uniformly at random and
duplicate it, creating a new node connected to the same nodes as
the old one.

The
density

D_{t}
of this network after
t
steps is the ratio
between the number of edges
m_{t}
and the number of possible edges

\binom{n_{t}}{2}
, where
n_{t}=n_{0}+t
is the number of nodes
(including the base station, even though it doesn’t otherwise
participate in the network).
We’d like to examine how the density evolves over time as new
nodes are added to the network.

An example of this process is given in
Figure
B.2
.

base
a
b

base
a
b
b^{\prime}

base
a
a^{\prime}
b
b^{\prime}

Figure B.2:
Example of graph density evolution. Initial
graph has density
D_{0}=1/\binom{3}{2}=1/3
. After duplicating

b
, new density is
D_{1}=2/\binom{4}{2}=1/3
. After
duplicating
a
as well,
final density is
D_{2}=4/\binom{5}{2}=2/5
.

1.

Compute the exact value of
\E\left[{D_{t}}\right]
as a function of

n
,
m
, and
t
.

2.

Show that, for any
t
,
D_{t}
is within
O\left(\sqrt{\log n/n}\right)
of
\E\left[{D_{t}}\right]

with high probability.

Solution

1.

We’ll show that
\left\{{D_{t}}\right\}
is a martingale, giving

\E\left[{D_{t}}\right]=\E\left[{D_{0}}\right]=m/\binom{n}{2}
for all

t
.

Let
G_{t}
be the graph after
t
steps.
Let
\mathcal{F}_{t}
be the
\sigma
-algebra generated by
\left\langle{G_{0},\dots,G_{t}}\right\rangle
.

Each edge in

G_{t}
goes between two non-base-station nodes, so
there is a chance of exactly
\frac{2}{n_{t}-1}
that
one of its endpoints is duplicated. Summing over all
edges gives

\E\left[{m_{t+1}}\;\middle|\;{m_{t}}\right]=m_{t}\left(1-\frac{2}{n-1}\right)
.
But then

\displaystyle\E\left[{D_{t+1}}\;\middle|\;{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\right]

\displaystyle=\frac{m_{t}\left(2\right){n-1}}{\binom{n_{t}+1}{2}}

\displaystyle=\frac{m_{t}\frac{n+1}{n-1}}{\binom{n_{t}+1}{2}\frac{n+1}{n-1}}

\displaystyle=\frac{m_{t}}{\binom{n_{t}}{2}}

\displaystyle=D_{t}.

It follows that
\E\left[{D_{t}}\right]=\E\left[{D_{0}}\right]=m/\binom{n}{2}
.

2.

We will apply Azuma’s inequality. This requires
getting bounds on the martingale differences
X_{t}=D_{t}-D_{t-1}
.

Since the maximum possible degree of any node in

G_{t-1}
is
n_{t-1}-2
, we have
m_{t}\leq m_{t-1}+n_{t-1}-2

and thus

\displaystyle D_{t}-D_{t-1}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{m_{t-1}+n_{t-1}-2}{\binom{n_{t-1}+1}{2}}-\frac{m_{t-1}}{\binom{n_{t-1}}{2}}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{m_{t-1}+n_{t-1}-2}{\binom{n_{t-1}}{2}}-\frac{m_{t-1}}{\binom{n_{t-1}}{2}}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{n_{t-1}}{\binom{n_{t-1}}{2}}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{2}{n_{t-1}-1}.

\displaystyle=\frac{2}{n+t-2}.

In the other direction, duplicating a node destroys no
edges, so
m_{t}\geq m_{t-1}
, giving

\displaystyle D_{t}-D_{t-1}

\displaystyle\geq\frac{m_{t-1}}{\binom{n_{t-1}+1}{2}}-\frac{m_{t-1}}{\binom{n_{t-1}}{2}}

\displaystyle=m_{t-1}\frac{\binom{n_{t-1}}{2}-\binom{n_{t-1}+1}{2}}{\binom{n_{t-1}+1}{2}\binom{n_{t-1}}{2}}

\displaystyle=m_{t-1}\frac{-n_{t-1}}{\binom{n_{t-1}+1}{2}\binom{n_{t-1}}{2}}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{-n_{t-1}}{\binom{n_{t-1}+1}{2}}

\displaystyle=-\frac{2}{n+t}.

So in either direction we have
\left\lvert X_{t}\right\rvert=\left\lvert D_{t+1}-D_{t}\right\rvert\leq\frac{2}{n+t-2}
.

Now let us apply Azuma’s inequality:

\displaystyle\Pr\left[{\left\lvert D_{t}-\E\left[{D_{t}}\right]\right\rvert\geq\alpha}\right]

\displaystyle\leq 2\exp\left(-\alpha^{2}/\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left(\frac{2}{n+i-2}\right)^{2}\right)

\displaystyle\leq 2\exp\left(-\alpha^{2}/\left(4\sum_{k=n-1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k^{2}}\right)\right)

\displaystyle\leq 2\exp\left(-\alpha^{2}/\left(4\int_{x=n-2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}\;dx\right)\right)

\displaystyle\leq 2\exp\left(-\alpha^{2}(n-2)/4\right).

For any fixed
c
, setting
\alpha=\sqrt{4(c+1)\ln n/(n-2)}=O\left(\sqrt{\log n/n}\right)
gives a
probability of at most
2n^{-c-1}\leq n^{-c}
(when

n\geq 2
) that we are more than
\alpha
away from the expectation.

B.3
Assignment 3, due Thursday 2023-04-27 at 23:59

B.3.1
Shuffling a graph

Consider the following shuffling algorithm:
Given a connected graph
G
with
n
vertices labeled
1
through
n
,
and
m
edges, at each step, with probability
1/2
, choose one of the edges uniformly at
random and swap the labels of its endpoints. This process yields a
Markov chain that is aperiodic and
irreducible,
2
2

2

Aperiodicity is immediate from having steps
that do nothing. For irreducibility, if
G
is a tree, there is at
least one vertex
v
with degree
1
; use a sequence of swaps to
move the desired label to
v
, then recurse on
G\setminus\left\{{v}\right\}
to
fix the rest of the labeling. For general
G
, apply this
procedure to a spanning tree of
G
.

so it has a unique
stationary distribution.

1.

What is the stationary distribution of this process?

2.

Show that this process converges to within a total
variation distance of
\epsilon
of its stationary distribution
in time polynomial in
n
and
\log\frac{1}{\epsilon}
.

Solution

1.

Suppose there is a labeling
i
and a labeling
j
such
that
j
is reachable from
i
in one step. Then these
labelings differ by swapping one edge so
p_{ij}=p_{ji}=\frac{1}{2m}
. For each labeling
i
, let
\pi_{i}=1/n!
. Then
\sum_{i}\pi_{i}=1
and, for all
i
and
j
,

\pi_{i}p_{ij}=\pi_{j}p_{ji}=\frac{m}{n!}
. This shows
that the chain is reversible and that this particular
\pi
is its
stationary distribution.

2.

We’ll do a coupling argument, similar to the
argument for adjacent-swap shuffling on a line. For
technical reasons that we will see later, it will be
helpful to assume that
G
has at least two edges. In
the case where
G
has only one edge, we can argue
that the process reaches the stationary distribution
in one step, as there are only two labelings and the
first step has a
1/2
chance each of switching or staying
put.

Let
X
and
Y
be two copies of the process, with
X

starting in an arbitrary distribution and
Y
starting
in the uniform stationary distribution.
At each step, let
D
be the set of edges with the
same label on at least one endpoint.
For each edge
uv
:

(a)

If
uv\in D
, swap
uv
in both copies with
probability
\frac{1}{2m}
.

(b)

If
uv\not\in D
, swap
uv
in
X
only with
probability
\frac{1}{2m}
and in
Y
only
with probability
\frac{1}{2m}
.

Do nothing with the remaining probability

\frac{\lvert D\rvert}{2m}
.

For each label
\ell
, write
X_{\ell}
for the vertex
labeled with
\ell
in
X
and
Y_{\ell}
for the vertex
labeled with
\ell
in
Y
. As in the adjacent-swap
case, we can argue that once
X_{\ell}=Y_{\ell}
, any
edge
uv
with an endpoint labeled
\ell
is in
D
,
so
X_{\ell}
continues to equal
Y_{\ell}
in all
subsequent states of the coupled process. So the
question then is how long it takes for two unlinked
copies of a label to become linked.

Define a new process
Z^{t}=\left\langle{U^{t},V^{t}}\right\rangle
where

U^{t}
represents the position
X^{t}_{\ell}
and
V^{t}

represents
Y^{t}_{\ell}
. Unlike the

\left\langle{X^{t}_{\ell},Y^{t}_{\ell}}\right\rangle
process, we will assume
that at each step of
Z^{t}
we always move
U^{t}
across
an incident edge with probability
\frac{1}{2n}
and
similarly for
V^{t}
, without regard to whether
U^{t}=V^{t}
. This gives a Markov chain with the same
transition probabilities as

\left\langle{X^{t}_{\ell},Y^{t}_{\ell}}\right\rangle
when
X^{t}_{\ell}\neq Y^{t}_{\ell}
, but unlike the
\left\langle{X^{t}_{\ell},Y^{t}_{\ell}}\right\rangle

process, the
Z^{t}
process is both irreducible and
reversible, with a uniform stationary distribution.
We can also argue that it is aperiodic under our
assumption that
m>1
, because there exists at least
one state where
U^{t}
is not adjacent to some
edge, so there is a nonzero probability that
Z_{t+1}=Z^{t}
in this state.

We will now show that
X^{t}_{\ell}
and
Y^{t}_{\ell}

collide with high probability after polynomially-many
steps by showing convergence of
Z^{t}
to its
stationary distribution using Cheeger’s inequality.
Observe that the
Z
chain has exactly
m^{2}
states,
and that each non-empty subset
S
of the chain has at
least one transition that leaves it with probability

\pi_{i}p_{ij}=\frac{1}{m^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{2m}=\frac{1}{2m^{3}}
. This gives

\Phi_{S}\geq\frac{1/2m^{3}}{\lvert S\rvert/m^{2}}
which is at
least
\frac{1}{4m^{3}}
in the worst case.
It follows that
\tau_{2}\leq\frac{2}{\Phi^{2}}\leq 8m^{6}
and
that the total variation distance between
Z^{t}
and
the uniform distribution is at most
\frac{1}{2m}

after
O(m^{6}\log m)
steps. In particular this gives
a probability of at least
\frac{1}{m}-\frac{1}{2m}=\frac{1}{2m}
of being in a state
\left\langle{U^{t},V^{t}}\right\rangle

with
U^{t}=V^{t}
at the end of each such interval.
Repeating for
O(m\log m)
intervals with a suitable
constant gives a probability of at most
m^{-c}
for
any fixed
c
that
U^{t}=V^{t}
at the end of one of
these intervals, which shows that
X_{\ell}
and

Y_{\ell}
collide within
O(m^{7}\log^{2}m)
steps with
probability at least
1-m^{-c}
.

Since
m\geq n-1
, we can choose
c
so that the
probability that
X_{\ell}
and
Y_{\ell}
don’t collide
in
O(m^{7}\log^{2}m)
steps is
O(n^{-2})
. By the
union bound, this gives that
X_{\ell}
and
Y_{\ell}

collide in time
O(m^{7}\log^{2}m)
with probability at
least
1-O(n^{-}1)
. Repeat as needed at most
O(\log(1/\epsilon))
times to drive the probability of failure down
below
\epsilon
, and use
m=O(n^{2})
to express the
convergence time in terms of
n
as
O(n^{1}4\log^{2}n\log(1/\epsilon))
. This polynomial in
n
and
\log\frac{1}{\epsilon}
even though the exponents are terrible.

B.3.2
Counting unbalanced sets

Suppose you are given the usual set balancing set-up, where you
have a collection of sets
S_{1},S_{2},\dots,S_{m}
with

\left\lvert\bigcup S_{i}\right\rvert=n
, and you are asked assign a value
\pm 1

to each element
x
of of
S=\bigcup S_{i}
with the goal of
minimizing the discrepancy
d=\max_{i}\left\lvert\sum_{x\in S_{i}}x\right\rvert
.

We know that applying a random assignment gives
d=O(\sqrt{n\log m})
with high probability. But this bound doesn’t take into
account any structure the
S_{i}
might have. Give a FPRAS
that takes the
S_{i}
as input along with a bound
t
and computes
an approximation for
\Pr\left[{d\geq t}\right]
, assuming each
x
is assigned

\pm 1
using an independent fair coin-flip.

Solution

Let
A
be the set of all assignments that produce
d\geq t
.
For each
i
, let
X_{i}=\sum_{x\in S_{i}}x
be the random variable representing
the sum of the assignments of elements of
S_{i}
.
We can write
A
as the union of
B_{ij}
for all
i\in[m]

and all
j
with
\lvert j\rvert\geq t
, where
B_{ij}
is the event
that
X_{i}=j
. Since this union is not disjoint, we
will use Karp-Luby (see
§
11.4
) to approximate its
size.

As with #DNF, the idea is that we can both count and
sample triples
\left\langle{i,j,x}\right\rangle
where
x

is an assignment that makes
X_{i}=j
. Let
n_{i}=\lvert S_{i}\rvert
. Let
Y_{i}
be the number of elements of
S_{i}
that
are assigned
+1
; then
X_{i}=Y_{i}-(n_{i}-Y_{i})=2Y_{i}-n_{i}
, and solving for
Y_{i}
gives
Y_{i}=\frac{n_{i}+X_{i}}{2}
,
assuming the numerator is even. Given
i
and
j
, there are
exactly
2^{n-n_{i}}\binom{n_{i}}{(n_{i}+j)/2}
assignments with

X_{i}=j
when
n_{i}+j
is even, and none when
n_{i}+j
is
odd. For the even case, we can sample these assignments in
polynomial time by choosing
(n_{i}+j)/2
elements without
replacement from
S_{i}
to have value
+1
, making the
remaining elements of
S_{i}
have value
-1
, and assigning

\pm 1
values independently to any
x\in S\setminus S_{i}
.
We will abuse notation slightly by writing
B_{ij}
for the
set of all possible triples
\left\langle{i,j,x}\right\rangle
resulting from
this process for a particular pair of values
i
and
j
.
Let
B=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\bigcup_{\lvert j\rvert\geq d,\text{$j+n_{i}$ even}}B_{ij}
; note that this union is
disjoint.

Our full sampling procedure looks like this:

1.

Sample
i
and
j
with probability
\lvert B_{ij}\rvert/\lvert B\rvert
.
Assuming that we precompute the sizes of the
B_{ij}

sets and that arithmetic operations take time
O(1)
time each, this takes
time at most
O(nm)
if we are naive about the
sampling and
O(\log nm)
if we are a little bit more
clever and use binary search.

2.

Sample an element
\left\langle{i,j,x}\right\rangle
of
B_{i}j
uniformly as described
above. This takes time
O(n)
.

3.

Return
1
if
x
does not appear in
B_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}
for
any
i^{\prime}j^{\prime}
that precedes
ij
in lexicographic order.
This requires checking
O(nm)
previous sets at a cost
of
O(n)
each, for
O(n^{2}m)
time total, which
dominates the cost of generating the sample.

Let
\rho
be the probability that we obtain
1
in an iteration
of this process. Then
\lvert A\rvert=\rho\lvert B\rvert
, and we can
approximate
\lvert A\rvert
to within relative error
\epsilon
by
approximating
\rho
within the same bound. Because each element
of
A
occurs in at least one and at most
O(nm)
of the

B_{ij}
, we have that
\rho=\Omega\left(\frac{1}{nm}\right)
.
Applying Lemma
11.2.1
,
approximating
\rho
using
N
samples where

N=\frac{3}{\epsilon^{2}\rho}\ln\frac{2}{\delta}=O\left(\frac{n^{2}m^{2}\log\delta}{\epsilon^{2}}\right)
gives us our desired error bounds in time
polynomial in
nm
,
1/\epsilon
, and
\log\delta
, as required.
